raw_case_text:
A twenty-five-year-old male patient from Paicandu, Parana, sought the health care unit of his city because of an ulcer on the lower lip that was treated as herpes labialis without wound healing or improvement. In August 2015, after thirty days of the ulcer appearance, the patient was referred to the LEPAC (Laboratorio de Ensino e Pesquisa em Analises Clinicas) at the Universidade Estadual de Maringa. During examination of the lower lip, an ulcerated lesion was observed, it was erythematous with raised edges and there was the presence of granulomatous, purulent and crusty contents characteristic of mucosal leishmaniasis (Figure 1A). In a patient interview, he described that he frequently fished in the Ivai river, an endemic region for Leishmania (Viannia) sp. and several acquaintances acquired leishmaniasis in the same place.
The conducted laboratory tests were Montenegro skin test, direct parasite search in the scraping from lesion edges and in the patient's blood sample an indirect immunofluorescence for anti-Leishmania IgG antibodies was performed. The Montenegro skin test was reactive with an induration of 6 mm in diameter, indirect immunofluorescence was positive for anti-Leishmania IgG antibodies with titer of 1:80 and the direct parasite search was also positive (Figure 1B). Detection of the parasite in the scraping from lesion edges and in the patient's blood sample were made by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) using primers to amplify a 70-bp fragment of the kinetoplast minicircle DNA (kDNA) from parasites belonging to Leishmania (Viannia) sp. subgenera. Only the scraping material was positive (Figure 1C).
The initial therapeutic regimen for treating leishmaniasis was Glucantime , three ampoules per day (1.215 mg) with four cycles of treatment: 20 and 30 days with an interval of 12 weeks, and two extra-cycles of 40 and 30 days with a break of approximately 10 days. This therapeutic scheme used by the patient is actually the one recommended to cutaneous leishmaniasis, since, according to what is suggested by the Brazilian Ministry of Health, the duration of the first cycle is 20 days with 10-20 mg/kg/day of Glucantime , respecting the limit of three ampoules per day, being repeated for more 30 days in case of failure with an interval of 12 weeks. At this stage, the patient was followed up by a new medical team, who decided not to use the therapeutic regimen recommended by the Ministry of Health, prescribing other two cycles of Glucantime , 40 and 30 days with an interval of approximately 10 days between them. The treatment with Glucantime  was unsuccessful, because the lesion reappeared with nodular aspect followed by ulceration. The side effects reported by the patient were present only on the first day of Glucantime  administration (seasickness and fever). Electrocardiogram was used to monitor the treatment side effects. In this situation, amphotericin B administration was necessary and 1 mg/kg/day was administered during 30 days with an interval of three days every 10 days, respecting the maximum of 50 mg (one flask) per administration.
Delayed diagnosis and treatment failure led the patient to episodes of depression. In March 2017, three months after treatment with amphotericin B and 19 months after correct diagnosis, the patient was in remission and under observation (Figure 1D). The project received the approval of the Project Management System (process No 1505/1997) of the Universidade Estadual de Maringa and the patient signed an informed consent form and a photograph consent form.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 25-year-old male presented with a 30-day non-healing ulcer on his lower lip.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 25-year-old male from Paiçandu, Paraná, Brazil presented with an ulcer on his lower lip that had persisted for 30 days. It was initially treated as herpes labialis without improvement, prompting referral to LEPAC at Universidade Estadual de Maringá in August 2015. He was treated with meglumine antimoniate (Glucantime, 3 ampoules/day) across four extended cycles (20, 30, 40, and 30 days), but treatment failed as the lesion recurred as a nodule that re-ulcerated. He experienced reactive depression due to diagnostic delay and repeated therapeutic failure, before successful second-line antimonial salvage.
subjective.past_medical_history: Frequent recreational fishing in the Ivaí river, an endemic area for Leishmania (Viannia) sp., where acquaintances had contracted leishmaniasis. No prior chronic diseases. Prior topical/systemic antiherpetic therapy without effect.
subjective.review_of_systems: Lower lip ulceration, nausea/seasickness and fever on first day of antimonial administration, depressive symptoms. Denied systemic fever, weight loss, or adenopathy.

objective.physical_examination: Physical examination of the lower lip revealed an erythematous ulcerated lesion with raised borders and granulomatous, purulent, and crusty exudate. Serial electrocardiograms (ECG) performed during antimonial therapy remained normal without QT prolongation.
objective.routine_investigations: Serial electrocardiograms (ECG) performed to monitor potential antimonial cardiotoxicity showed normal tracings.
objective.advanced_workup: Scraping from the lesion margins stained with Giemsa: microscopic examination revealed intracellular microorganisms. Blood and scraping samples subjected to molecular testing.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive Diagnosis: Mucosal leishmaniasis of the lower lip caused by Leishmania (Viannia) sp., refractory to pentavalent antimony.
Diagnostic Confirmation: Direct parasite search in lesion scraping revealed Leishmania amastigotes; Montenegro skin test was reactive (induration 6 mm); indirect immunofluorescence was positive for anti-Leishmania IgG (titer 1:80); PCR amplifying a 70-bp kDNA minicircle fragment of subgenus Leishmania (Viannia) was positive on lesion scraping (negative in blood).
Differentials Ruled Out: Herpes labialis (initial misdiagnosis, unresponsive to antivirals), squamous cell carcinoma, paracoccidioidomycosis, and primary syphilis.
Treatment & Clinical Course: Patient failed extensive therapy with Glucantime (3 ampoules/day = 1,215 mg over 4 cycles of 20, 30, 40, and 30 days) with lesion recurrence. Salvage therapy with intravenous amphotericin B (1 mg/kg/day, maximum 50 mg/day, for 30 days with 3-day intervals every 10 days) was instituted, resulting in complete mucosal healing and sustained remission at 19-month follow-up.
